about: Data of Learn lesson A16, Where does hydrogen make sense? The wind farm, its grid limit and the hydrogen user are fictional and illustrative; the wind follows the real hourly shape of the Southwest Power Pool grid in 2025 (town_year.json, EIA-930). Every cost is in 2022 dollars, from one DOE record. Sources and dates are given with each item.

dataset.creator: Honglin Li
dataset.status: Illustrative: the wind farm, its grid limit and the hydrogen user are fictional; the wind follows SPP's real 2025 hourly shape (EIA-930); the costs are from one DOE record, in 2022 dollars.
dataset.source: Values for lesson A16 from the sources named with each item; the farm, its grid limit and the hydrogen user are set for teaching.
dataset.license: CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), Honglin Li. Values taken from the sources named in this file keep their publishers' terms; EIA and DOE data are U.S. government works in the public domain.

farm.note: Illustrative: a 100 MW wind farm whose grid connection takes at most 50 MW. Its hours are constructed, not measured: SPP's regional 2025 shape raised to a power so the peak hour reaches 100 MW and the year averages 33.8%; spare wind and the tank depend on that construction.

electrolyzer.doeBoundary: DOE's $5-7/kg (Record 24005, pp. 1-2 and the appendix) counts fixed upkeep (5% of the installed cost a year) and stack replacement (11% of it every 40,000 operating hours); it leaves out compression, storage, distribution and dispensing, and assumes 50-75% capacity factors and about 10% nominal cost of capital. The lesson counts capital and power only, at 4% real.

source.label: DOE Hydrogen Program Record 24005, Clean Hydrogen Production Cost Scenarios with PEM Electrolyzer Technology, Table 1 and p. 1 (2022 dollars)

loadSource.label: IRENA, Green Hydrogen Cost Reduction (2020), Table 6: load range of PEM 5%–120%, of alkaline 15%–100%

elecPriceNote: DOE's record assumes renewable electricity at roughly $0.03/kWh (2022 dollars); the lesson uses it as the value of a MWh of wind the farm could have sold, and as the price of grid power.

lhvSource.label: DOE Hydrogen Program Plan (December 2024), p. 24: the energy content of hydrogen is 33 kWh/kg, lower heating value

fuelCellSource.label: DOE, Fuel Cells: efficiencies capable of exceeding 60%

gridCO2Note: Illustrative: in the hours the farm's wind falls short, the extra grid power is assumed to come from a gas combined-cycle plant like Prairie Town's (0.37 t CO2 per MWh, operating emissions only).

chpsSource.label: DOE, Clean Hydrogen Production Standard Guidance (June 2023), p. 2: a target of at most 4.0 kg CO2e per kg of hydrogen, well-to-gate; pp. 2-3: the example of a gas reformer with about 95% capture, on the average U.S. grid mix and with upstream methane emissions of at most 1%

cavernSource.label: DOE Loan Programs Office, Advanced Clean Energy Storage environmental assessment (DOE/EA-2182, April 2022), §2.2: each salt cavern about 5,000 t of hydrogen

cards.why: Ammonia is made from hydrogen: about 60% of industry's 55 Mt of hydrogen in 2024 (IEA).
Refineries already use over 43 Mt a year (IEA, 2024): the choice is how it is made.

cards.text: Steel from iron ore (hydrogen-based direct reduction)
cards.why: Hydrogen can replace the gas that strips oxygen from the ore; about 10% of industry's hydrogen today (IEA). Electricity-only routes are still in development.
Long voyages need dense fuels; ammonia and methanol made from hydrogen compete with others.
Salt caverns hold weeks of energy cheaply, but little comes back: about 35% here (step 1), 31% in DOE's 2022 storage assessment (A8).

cards.text: Long-haul trucks, on routes longer than today's batteries cover
cards.why: Where batteries do not yet cover the route, fuel cells and batteries are both tried; a battery truck still uses far less electricity per mile.
Electric car: 100 miles on 25–40 kWh. Fuel cell car: about 60 miles per kg, made with 57 kWh: about 1 mile per kWh.
A heat pump gives up to three times the heat of the power it uses; hydrogen loses about 40% before any heat is made.

sources.label: IEA, Global Hydrogen Review 2025, pp. 41 and 48
